content: 1. In community settings, it is essential to evaluate both the impact and the sustained effectiveness of interventions that rely on antimicrobial prophylaxis. 2. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent perinatal Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease is indicated under a universal prenatal screening strategy. This strategy involves collecting combined vaginal and rectal cultures from all pregnant women between 35 and 37 weeks of gestation. 3. If labor begins or the amniotic membranes rupture before 37 weeks of gestation, and there is a significant risk of preterm delivery as determined by the clinician, a recommended algorithm for GBS prophylaxis management should be followed. 4. If chorioamnionitis is suspected, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy that includes an agent effective against GBS should replace standard GBS prophylaxis. 5. Intrapartum prophylaxis is not indicated in the following scenarios: A previous pregnancy with a positive GBS screening culture, unless the current pregnancy also has a positive culture. Planned cesarean delivery performed without labor or membrane rupture, regardless of maternal GBS culture status. Negative vaginal and rectal GBS screening cultures during late gestation in the current pregnancy, even if intrapartum risk factors are present. 6. Anaphylaxis associated with GBS chemoprophylaxis is rare. The morbidity associated with anaphylaxis is significantly outweighed by the reduction in maternal and neonatal invasive GBS disease. 7. Mortality from anaphylaxis is likely to be a rare event, as women receiving intrapartum antibiotics are in hospital settings where rapid intervention is readily available. 8. The estimated rate of anaphylaxis caused by penicillin ranges from 4 per 10,000 to 4 per 100,000 recipients. Additionally, up to 10% of the adult population may experience less severe allergic reactions to penicillin. 9. Anaphylaxis related to GBS prophylaxis was first reported in the early 1990s. Since the release of the 1996 guidelines, there has been one additional report of a nonfatal case of anaphylaxis associated with GBS chemoprophylaxis. 10. In a CDC multistate sample of over 5,000 live births, a single nonfatal anaphylactic reaction was observed among the 27% of deliveries where intrapartum antibiotics were administered. In this case, the reaction occurred shortly after the mother received a single dose of a cephalosporin following umbilical cord clamping. 11. To date, no GBS isolates with confirmed resistance to penicillin or ampicillin have been observed. Penicillin remains the preferred agent for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis due to its narrower antimicrobial spectrum and lower likelihood of selecting for resistant organisms. Ampicillin is an acceptable alternative. 12. Both penicillin and ampicillin have demonstrated efficacy as intrapartum agents for preventing early-onset neonatal GBS disease in clinical trials. Intravenous administration is the only recommended route for intrapartum chemoprophylaxis, as it achieves higher intraamniotic concentrations compared to intramuscular administration. 13. Since 1996, the proportion of GBS isolates with in vitro resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin has increased. Reports from the United States and Canada between 1998 and 2001 indicate resistance rates ranging from 7% to 25% for erythromycin and 3% to 15% for clindamycin. 14. Resistance to erythromycin is frequently, but not always, associated with clindamycin resistance. Resistance to cefoxitin, a second-generation cephalosporin sometimes used for broad-spectrum coverage in chorioamnionitis, has also been reported. 15. The clinical implications of in vitro resistance of GBS remain unclear.
